Introduction to Psychopharmacology  |  Lecture 2

Neurons and their messengers

How neurons signal, the synapse, the chemical messengers and where drugs act

Leonard, Fundamentals of Psychopharmacology (3rd ed.), Chapter 2 (and the end of Chapter 1)

Part 5

How neurons signal

Inside a neuron the message is electrical. Between neurons it becomes chemical.

At rest, a neuron is a charged battery

Charged particles (ions) are unevenly spread: more sodium outside, more potassium inside.

A pump keeps it that way, using energy.

The result: the inside sits at about −70 millivolts compared with the outside. This is the resting potential.

Ion channels are protein pores that open to let particular ions through. Opening them changes the voltage.

Illustration: Neurotorium, adapted from Human Physiology, University of Guelph (CC BY)

Ion channels: tiny doors that decide everything

Large proteins forming a pore through the membrane.

Each is selective: the width of the pore and the charges lining it decide which ion gets through (sodium, potassium, calcium or chloride).

Some open when the voltage changes; some open when a transmitter binds.

Most are built from 3 to 5 protein sub-units.

Changing even one amino acid can make a channel stay open longer or carry more current.

Why it matters

Small genetic differences in channels and receptors are one reason people respond differently to the same drug.

Try it: fire an action potential

Set the size of the push from other neurons, then stimulate.

Stimulus+8 mV

All or none

Reach threshold and the neuron fires a full, identical spike. Stronger input means more spikes per second, not bigger ones.

Part 6

The synapse

Where electricity becomes chemistry, and where most drugs do their work.

A gap with a name

Charles Sherrington proposed that nerve cells pass messages by releasing a chemical into a small space next to the next cell. He called the junction the synapse.

He predicted two things: the message goes one way only, and it is delayed by a few milliseconds while the chemical crosses the gap.

Both turned out to be right.

Charles Scott Sherrington, Bain News Service. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

An experiment that came in a dream

1921. Otto Loewi wakes with an idea, scribbles it down, and cannot read his handwriting in the morning. The next night the dream returns.

Step 1. Stimulate the vagus nerve of a frog heart in a dish. The heart slows.

Step 2. Move the fluid around that heart onto a second heart with no nerve stimulation. It slows too.

Conclusion. The nerve released a chemical. He called it Vagusstoff. We call it acetylcholine

Loewi shared the 1936 Nobel Prize with Henry Dale. Chemical transmission was proven first in the autonomic nerves, then found in the brain.

Otto Loewi, photograph by Albert Hilscher. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

What counts as a neurotransmitter? The detective’s checklist

1 Present in nerve terminals, in the region where it is thought to act

2 Released when the nerve is stimulated, usually needing calcium

3 Made and destroyed nearby: the enzymes that build and break it are in or near the terminal

4 Same effect when applied directly as when released naturally

5 Drug-sensitive: blocked by a specific antagonist and mimicked by a specific agonist

Leonard treats these as guidelines, not strict rules. Criterion 5 shows how closely drugs and transmitters are tied together.

Synaptic transmission, step by step

A neuron is a vote-counter

0spikes fired

A hippocampal granule cell listens to up to 10,000 inputs. Excitatory ones land on the dendrites; fewer inhibitory ones sit by the cell body, where they can veto. Inputs fade quickly, so they only add up when they arrive close together.

Two kinds of receptor: a door and a doorbell

Ionotropic: the door

The receptor is an ion channel. Transmitter binds, the channel opens: milliseconds.

Glutamate, GABA, glycine, acetylcholine (nicotinic)

Metabotropic: the doorbell

The receptor passes the message inside via a G-protein. Slower, longer-lasting, with wider effects.

Noradrenaline, dopamine, serotonin, acetylcholine (muscarinic), peptides

Illustration: Neurotorium, Lundbeck Foundation

Inside the doorbell: the second-messenger chain

Amplification: one transmitter molecule can lead to thousands of cAMP molecules.

Some G-proteins stimulate the chain (Gs), others inhibit it (Gi).

Example

Dopamine D1 receptors turn cAMP up. D2 receptors turn it down. Same transmitter, opposite effect.

Locks and keys: how drugs talk to receptors

Receptor activity

The idea of receptors goes back to J. N. Langley (1905), who noticed drugs could copy or cancel the body’s own signals.

Autoreceptors: the terminal’s own thermostat

Receptors sit on the releasing terminal itself. When transmitter builds up in the cleft, they tell the terminal to release less.

For noradrenaline these are α2 receptors.

Clonidine (α2 agonist) turns release down. Yohimbine (α2 antagonist) turns it up.

Heteroceptors (H) respond to other transmitters: serotonin can boost noradrenaline release, for example.

Receptors adapt to what they are given

Receptors on the cell surface: 10

Why antidepressants are slow

The drug acts on the synapse within hours, but mood improves over weeks. The slow receptor changes are thought to be part of the reason.

Messengers travel in pairs: co-transmission

acetylcholine

+ vasoactive intestinal peptide

dopamine

+ cholecystokinin

serotonin

+ substance P

Peptides are different

  • At least 40 kinds in the brain
  • Stored in larger vesicles
  • Act at tiny concentrations
  • Mostly slow: they tune the main transmitter’s effect

Some act alone too

Enkephalins, endorphins, substance P, vasopressin and others act as transmitters in their own right. Some mimic morphine.

The chemical messengers

Meet the main cast: what each one does, where it lives, and which drugs act on it.

glutamate

Glutamate: the main accelerator

The brain’s chief excitatory transmitter, found throughout the brain. It is also used in ordinary metabolism, and is the raw material for GABA.

  • AMPA and kainate receptors: fast excitation
  • NMDA receptors: slower; key for learning and memory. Glycine helps them work
  • Metabotropic (8 types): slow modulation
Too much of a good thing

After a stroke, excess glutamate overexcites neurons to death (excitotoxicity).

from the cortex to deeper areas

Pathway illustrations: Neurotorium, Lundbeck Foundation

GABA: the main brake

GABA

The chief inhibitory transmitter, at over 40% of synapses in the cortex by Leonard’s estimate.

Made from glutamate by the enzyme GAD. After release it is taken back into neurons and glia, then broken down by GABA transaminase.

Too little GABA activity: seizures and anxiety.

GABA-A

A chloride channel (fast). Target of benzodiazepines, barbiturates and alcohol.

GABA-B

G-protein receptor (slow). Target of baclofen, a muscle relaxant.

Breakdown blockers

Valproate and vigabatrin raise GABA and are used against epilepsy.

The GABA-A receptor: one channel, many drugs

Like a single-channel recording: each block is one opening.

acetylcholine

Acetylcholine: memory and attention

Built from choline + acetyl-CoA. Destroyed in the cleft by acetylcholinesterase.

Fibres from the nucleus basalis of Meynert spread across the cortex. This area is damaged in Alzheimer’s disease.

Eating extra choline does not help: the supply into the terminal is already running at full speed.

Enzyme blockers

Physostigmine reaches the brain; neostigmine does not. Irreversible blockers are insecticides and nerve gases.

Basal forebrain (nucleus basalis) cortex

Receptors named after a mushroom and a plant

Henry Dale noticed that acetylcholine could mimic two natural poisons: muscarine, from toadstools like the fly agaric, and nicotine, from tobacco.

Nicotinic

Ion channel, fast. Muscles, and some brain areas.

Muscarinic (M1–M5)

G-protein, slow. Heart, glands, and much of the brain. Blocked by atropine.

Fly agaric (Amanita muscaria), Holger Krisp, Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 3.0)

Making dopamine and noradrenaline: an assembly line

phenylalanine tyrosine tyrosine hydroxylase: the slowest step L-DOPA dopa decarboxylase dopamine dopamine β-hydroxylase noradrenaline adrenaline

Rate-limiting step

The slowest enzyme sets the pace. It is normally working flat out, so extra dietary tyrosine does not make more dopamine.

Breakdown

MAO (monoamine oxidase) inside the neuron, and COMT in the cleft. MAO inhibitors are antidepressants.

Drug links

Carbidopa blocks dopa decarboxylase outside the brain. Disulfiram blocks dopamine β-hydroxylase (and alcohol breakdown).

SN / VTA Nigrostriatal Mesolimbic Mesocortical Tuberoinfundibular
dopamine

Dopamine: four highways

Nigrostriatal: movement. Lost in Parkinson’s disease.

Mesolimbic: reward and emotion. Overactive in psychosis.

Mesocortical: thinking and motivation.

Tuberoinfundibular: keeps prolactin release down.

D1-like (D1, D5): cAMP up. D2-like (D2, D3, D4): cAMP down. Antipsychotic strength tracks how well a drug blocks D2.

noradrenaline

Noradrenaline: alertness and drive

Most brain noradrenaline starts in the locus coeruleus, about 10,000 cells in the pons, and fans out to the cortex, thalamus, hypothalamus and hippocampus.

Linked to drive, motivation, reward, dreaming (REM) sleep, attention and mood: all disturbed in depression and mania.

Receptors: α1, α2 (the autoreceptor), β1, β2.

Locus coeruleus

Brain: Neurotorium, Lundbeck Foundation. Pathways drawn for this lecture.

Raphe nuclei to spinal cord (pain)
serotonin (5-HT)

Serotonin: the fine-tuner

From the raphe nuclei to almost everywhere. Mood, sleep, appetite, impulsivity, aggression, pain, sex.

tryptophanslowest step5-HTP→5-HTMAO →5-HIAA

Here the slowest enzyme is not working flat out, so tryptophan supply matters.

Tryptophan depletion: a drink of amino acids without tryptophan can quickly bring back depression in recovered patients.

Seven families of serotonin receptor, and the drugs that use them

ReceptorWhat it doesDrug example
5-HT1AInhibitory; anxiety and moodBuspirone (agonist): anti-anxiety
5-HT1B/1DInhibitory, on nerve terminalsSumatriptan (agonist): migraine
5-HT2APerception, moodLSD: hallucinations
5-HT2CAppetite, sexual functionLinked to SSRI sexual side effects
5-HT3The only ion-channel type; vomitingOndansetron (antagonist): anti-sickness
5-HT4 to 5-HT7Less certainSeveral antipsychotics and antidepressants bind them

Psychopharmacology’s origin story: in the 1950s Woolley and Shaw suggested LSD works by interfering with serotonin, because the two molecules look alike.

Nitric oxide: the rule-breaker

nitric oxide

A gas, made on demand from the amino acid arginine. It is not stored in vesicles.

It passes straight through membranes, and can travel backwards, from the receiving cell to the sending cell.

Why it matters

In the hippocampus it tells the sending cell to release more glutamate, strengthening the connection (long-term potentiation). Blocking it impairs memory formation in experiments.

Recap: the brain’s chemical wiring

Part 8

Where drugs act

Putting it together: every step of transmission is a place to intervene.

The drug toolbox: seven places to intervene

1 Synthesis: block or feed the assembly line (carbidopa, L-DOPA)

2 Storage: stop vesicles filling

3 Release: more or less transmitter per signal

4 Receptors: agonists and antagonists (antipsychotics block D2)

5 Reuptake: leave transmitter in the cleft longer (SSRIs)

6 Breakdown: block the enzyme (MAO inhibitors, anticholinesterases)

7 Autoreceptors: remove the thermostat (yohimbine)

Receptor profiles predict side effects

Binding studies show which receptors a drug blocks. From that list we can predict much of what patients will feel.

Blocks:

Or try a profile:

Simplified profiles for teaching.

Less psychosisthe intended effect of antipsychotics
Stiffness, tremor, restlessnessmovement side effects
Raised prolactinbreast changes, missed periods
Sedation, drowsinesslike old antihistamines
Dry mouth, blurred visionanticholinergic effects
Constipation, urinary retentionanticholinergic effects
Dizziness on standingpostural hypotension
Confusion, memory problemsespecially in older people

How do we know all this?

Radioligand binding

A radioactive drug sticks to receptors in brain tissue; counting it gives receptor numbers. Showed antipsychotic strength matches D2 binding.

Autoradiography

Brain slices exposed to film show where a labelled drug binds.

PET and SPECT

The only ways to see drug and receptor binding in a living human brain.

MRI and fMRI

Structure over time, and which areas are active during a task.

MR spectroscopy

Measures chemicals such as GABA and glutamate. Found lower GABA in depression.

TMS

Magnetic pulses stimulate the cortex. Tests cause and effect; a modest treatment for depression.

A binding site is not automatically a receptor: it must be shown to produce a response. It took years to prove the benzodiazepine binding site was real.

Final check

Five ideas to take away

1. Region, cell and molecule are linked: drugs act on molecules and change functions.

2. The blood–brain barrier decides which drugs reach the brain at all.

3. Inside neurons signals are electrical; between them they are chemical.

4. The receptor, not the transmitter, decides the effect.

5. Every step of transmission is a drug target, and the brain adapts to drugs over time.
